As Long As I Could See It Working. | Proxima SF", "meta-description": "I said I had faith. And I did — as long as I could reasonably see it happening. That's not quite the same thing.", "author": "699e12d16ef041f10a195450", "item-category": "69c08fd080415a7553051e0c", "tabs": [ "69c085d28383a3710d83adf6", "69c09dca3cac7986ad2990b4", "69c09def8ca16615fa39c126", "69c09e12ceecbebcef08d176" ], "main-content": "

I had it all mapped out.

We were excited — genuinely excited — about what the coming year held. I could see what God was doing. I had the vision, the team, the next steps. And I had the faith to match.

Then, without any warning, the plan fell apart.

Not slowly. Not with signals I could have caught earlier. Just — gone.

What surprised me wasn't the disruption itself. It was the confession it pulled out of me. Because when I was honest, I had to admit something: my faith had been real — but it had also been reasonable. I could see how it might work. I could trace the path from here to there. The faith and the forecast had been pointing in the same direction, and I hadn't noticed how much the second one was carrying the first.

That's an uncomfortable thing to sit with. But I think it's the right one.

We confuse a responsible plan with proof that God is in it. Responsibility matters — I'm not arguing for carelessness. But sometimes what God asks for doesn't look responsible. It doesn't fit the timeline. It moves before the conditions are right. And that's exactly what makes it hard to call faith.

Wisdom is willing to move when the time is right. Comfort waits until the outcome is predictable. I've confused the two more times than I'd like to admit — because waiting for certainty is easy to dress up as faithfulness. But faithfulness and forecasting are not the same posture, even when they look the same from the outside.

Faith that only functions when the outcome is visible isn't really faith — it's optimism with good theology attached. Certainty isn't about seeing the path clearly. It's about knowing the One who holds it. And what I know — who I know — doesn't change when the plan falls apart.

When the path forward costs something real, \"The Lord is my light and my salvation\" stops being a verse I know and becomes a choice I make. Faith is not recklessness. It is courageous surrender — stepping forward carefully, but stepping forward nonetheless, trusting that God provides what aligns with His will.

The question is simple and not easy: do I have faith, or do I have faith in what I can reasonably see happening?

Because those two things feel identical — right up until the plan falls apart.
